question.:question/problem:
Simplify the trigonometric expression $$
\displaystyle \frac{6\,\sin^{5} \theta\,\cos^{2} \theta+6\,\sin^{3} \theta\,\cos^{4} \theta}{\sin^{2} \theta\,\cos^{3} \theta}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we factor the numerator:

$$
\begin{aligned}&\frac{6\,\sin^{5} \theta\,\cos^{2} \theta+6\,\sin^{3} \theta\,\cos^{4} \theta}{\sin^{2} \theta\,\cos^{3} \theta} \\ &=\frac{6\,\sin^{3} \theta\,\cos^{2} \theta\,(\sin^{2} \theta+\cos^{2} \theta)}{\sin^{2} \theta\,\cos^{3} \theta}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we use the Pythagorean identity to rewrite the expression in the parentheses, and then we simplify the resulting expression as much as possible.

$$
\begin{aligned}&\frac{6\,\sin^{3} \theta\,\cos^{2} \theta\,(\sin^{2} \theta+\cos^{2} \theta)}{\sin^{2} \theta\,\cos^{3} \theta} \\ &=\frac{6\,\sin^{3} \theta\,\cos^{2} \theta\cdot 1}{\sin^{2} \theta\,\cos^{3} \theta} \\ &=\frac{6\,\sin^{3} \theta\,\cos^{2} \theta}{\sin^{2} \theta\,\cos^{3} \theta} \\ &=\frac{6\,\cancel{\sin^{2} \theta\,\cos^{2} \theta}\,\sin \theta}{\cancel{\sin^{2} \theta\,\cos^{2} \theta}\,\cos \theta} \\ &=\frac{6\,\sin \theta}{\cos \theta} \\ &=6\,\tan \theta\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}&\frac{6\,\sin^{5} \theta\,\cos^{2} \theta+6\,\sin^{3} \theta\,\cos^{4} \theta}{\sin^{2} \theta\,\cos^{3} \theta} \\ &=6\,\tan \theta\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Simplify the trigonometric expression $1+\frac{(1)\cdot (\sin^{2} \alpha)}{2+\cos^{2} \alpha}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We put both terms over a common denominator, and combine the two fractions. Then we expand the numerator, group the squared terms, and use the Pythagorean identity:

$$
\begin{aligned}& \frac{(2+\cos^{2} \alpha)+\sin^{2} \alpha}{2+\cos^{2} \alpha} \\ & =\frac{2+\cos^{2} \alpha+\sin^{2} \alpha}{2+\cos^{2} \alpha} \\ & =\frac{2+(\cos^{2} \alpha+\sin^{2} \alpha)}{2+\cos^{2} \alpha} \\ & =\frac{(2+1)}{2+\cos^{2} \alpha} \\ & =\frac{3}{2+\cos^{2} \alpha}\end{aligned}
$$

Here we used $\cos^{2} \alpha+\sin^{2} \alpha=1$. Therefore, the expression simplifies to $\frac{3}{2+\cos^{2} \alpha}$.

question.:question/problem: Simplify the trigonometric expression $\frac{-2\cdot \sin^{2} t}{1-\cos t}+3\cdot \cos t.$

question.:question/problem: Simplify the trigonometric expression $\frac{1+2\cdot \cos \alpha}{\sin \alpha}+4\cdot \tan \alpha.$
question.:question/worked-solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}& \frac{1+2\cdot \cos \alpha}{\sin \alpha}+4\cdot \tan \alpha \\ &= \frac{1+2\cdot \cos \alpha}{\sin \alpha}+\frac{4\cdot \sin \alpha}{\cos \alpha}\end{aligned}

Put both terms over a common denominator and combine the fractions:

$$
\begin{aligned}& \frac{(1+2\cdot \cos \alpha)\cos \alpha}{\sin \alpha\cdot \cos \alpha}+\frac{4\cdot \sin^{2} \alpha}{\sin \alpha\cdot \cos \alpha} \\ &= \frac{\cos \alpha+2\cdot \cos^{2} \alpha+4\cdot \sin^{2} \alpha}{\sin \alpha\cdot \cos \alpha}\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}& \frac{\cos \alpha+4\cdot (\cos^{2} \alpha+\sin^{2} \alpha)-2\cdot \cos^{2} \alpha}{\sin \alpha\cdot \cos \alpha} \\ &= \frac{\cos \alpha+4-2\cdot \cos^{2} \alpha}{\sin \alpha\cdot \cos \alpha}\end{aligned}
$$

\displaystyle \frac{\cos \alpha+4-2\cdot \cos^{2} \alpha}{\sin \alpha\cdot \cos \alpha},

question.:question/problem: Simplify the trigonometric expression $\frac{3\cdot \sin t}{1-\cos t}-2\cdot \cot t.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, rewrite the second term using $\cot t=\frac{\cos t}{\sin t}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}& \frac{3\cdot \sin t}{1-\cos t}-2\cdot \cot t \\ &= \frac{3\cdot \sin t}{1-\cos t}+\frac{-2\cdot \cos t}{\sin t}\end{aligned}
$$

Put both terms over a common denominator and combine the fractions:

$$
\begin{aligned}& \frac{3\cdot \sin^{2} t}{(1-\cos t)\sin t}+\frac{-2\cdot (\cos t(1-\cos t))}{(1-\cos t)\sin t} \\ &= \frac{3\cdot \sin^{2} t-2\cdot \cos t+2\cdot \cos^{2} t}{(1-\cos t)\sin t}\end{aligned}
$$

Group the squared terms and apply the Pythagorean identity. Then factor the numerator and cancel the common linear factor, retaining the original denominator exclusions.

$$
\begin{aligned}& \frac{3\cdot (\sin^{2} t+\cos^{2} t)-2\cdot \cos t-\cos^{2} t}{(1-\cos t)\sin t} \\ &= \frac{3-2\cdot \cos t-\cos^{2} t}{(1-\cos t)\sin t} \\ &= \frac{3\cdot (1-\cos t)+(\cos t(1-\cos t))}{(1-\cos t)\sin t} \\ &= \frac{(1-\cos t)(3+\cos t)}{(1-\cos t)\sin t} \\ &= \frac{3+\cos t}{\sin t}\end{aligned}
$$

Here we used $\cos^{2} t+\sin^{2} t=1$. Therefore, the simplified expression is $\frac{3+\cos t}{\sin t}$, on the original domain $\sin t\ne0, 1-\cos t\ne0$.
